Extraction: Generative AI revolution in cybersecurity: a comprehensive review of threat intelligence and operations
Mueen Uddin; Muhammad Saad Irshad; Irfan Ali Kandhro; Fuhid Alanazi; Fahad Ahmed; Muhammad Maaz; Saddam Hussain; Syed Sajid Ullah
2025; Artificial Intelligence Review (Springer), vol. 58, article 236; DOI 10.1007/s10462-025-11219-5; published online 7 May 2025

Cyber threats are increasingly frequent and organizations struggle to protect data from cybercriminals, while traditional cybersecurity methods (signature-based detection, manual analysis, education) are resource-intensive, limited by human cognition, and prone to human error; the survey targets the lack of a consolidated understanding of the opportunities and risks of Generative AI (GAI) in cybersecurity defense (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 1, pp. 2-3; Sec. 3.6, p. 9)

No new system is proposed (survey); it reviews GAI/LLM uses in cybersecurity — threat intelligence and threat hunting, honeypots, phishing detection and resilience training, vulnerability scanning/filtering, automated incident response — plus customized security LLMs (Sec-PaLM, SlashNext Generative Human AI, Big Data AI LLM) and commercial LLM copilots: SentinelOne Purple AI (GPT-4-based natural-language threat hunting), Google Cloud Security AI Workbench (Sec-PaLM; Chronicle AI, Security Command Center AI), and Microsoft Security Copilot (OpenAI GPT-4 plus proprietary security models, prompt books, human-in-the-loop: "rather than taking the position of security experts, its main objective is to support them") (Sec. 3, pp. 3-14; Sec. 4, pp. 17-19; Sec. 5, pp. 19-24)

Comprehensive narrative literature review (survey); positions itself against five related GAI-security surveys (Table 1) and organizes evidence into application taxonomies, customized LLMs, real-world tools, a 2023-2024 impact analysis, limitations, and future directions; systematic search protocol, databases, inclusion criteria, dataset, and sample size: Not specified (Table 1, p. 4; Fig. 1, p. 6; Secs. 3-9, pp. 3-33)

No quantitative MTTD/MTTR, alert-fatigue, or resolution-time results reported (Not specified); qualitative claims only: ChatGPT-generated hunting queries may yield "a quicker reaction time to the cyber-attack situation" (Sec. 3.7, p. 10); LLM threat-hunting queries improve "the system's efficiency and response time" (Sec. 3.9, p. 10); AI approaches give "Efficient analyst resources, automated, faster response" vs. manual DDoS monitoring (Table 2, p. 11); GAI "helps speed the response to any cyber incident" via automated incident response (Sec. 6.4, p. 25)

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: Multi-agent systems are not addressed; coverage is limited to single LLM assistants/copilots: GAI can "handle everyday threat situations autonomously" while augmenting humans in critical aspects (Abstract, p. 1); Microsoft Security Copilot is explicitly human-in-the-loop support, processes 65 trillion signals daily, and logs all prompts/responses for auditing (Sec. 5.9, p. 21); reported failure modes and costs include occasional incorrect/hallucinated results, expensive training, setup times of weeks to months, prompt-injection risk, poor interpretability, and no standardized empirical evaluation of GAI security tools (Sec. 7.1-7.3, p. 26; Table 3, p. 16; Sec. 7.14.1, p. 29)

Author-acknowledged GAI limitations: wrong/unethical outputs, cost inefficiency, high setup time (weeks to months of training), easy exploitability by malicious actors, weak interpretability/explainability, contextual and long-range-dependency limits, multi-turn conversation failures, data-privacy risks (breaches, inadequate anonymization, bias, lack of consent), lack of user control, and need for empirical evaluation (Sec. 7, pp. 26-29); future directions: automating cybersecurity, big-data threat intelligence, attack simulation for training, biometric security and privacy, fraud detection, blockchain data transparency, and future-proofing defenses (Sec. 9, pp. 31-33)

The paper maps the commercial landscape of LLM-based security copilots (Microsoft Security Copilot, SentinelOne Purple AI, Google Cloud Security AI Workbench), motivating the copilot paradigm my thesis transfers to SRE incident response. Its automated-incident-response discussion and repeated qualitative "faster response" claims support the hypothesis that LLM assistants can reduce detection and resolution times, yet it supplies no MTTD/MTTR evidence — reinforcing the measurement gap my RSL documents. Its explicit finding that GAI security tools lack standardized empirical evaluation strengthens the justification for a metric-driven (MTTD/MTTR) evaluation design. The limitation catalogue (hallucination, cost, explainability, prompt injection) feeds the risk and threats-to-validity analysis for an Agentic AI copilot.
Medium — adjacent work: it surveys single-agent LLM security copilots and automated incident response qualitatively, but offers no MTTD/MTTR measurements and no agentic/multi-agent architectures.
